explanations.explanation: Women it is, friend. Solomon, Israel's king, had every kind of treasure, and the text still points at his heart: “King Solomon, however, loved many foreign women along with the daughter of Pharaoh…” (1 Kings 11:1). That little “however” turns the whole story.

Good guess for a king, but the verse isn't about kingdoms. Solomon, Israel's king, loved “…many foreign women…” (1 Kings 11:1). Moab, Ammon, Edom and Sidon show up only as the places those women were from.

Cities aren't what he loved, friend. The text says King Solomon “…loved many foreign women along with the daughter of Pharaoh…” (1 Kings 11:1). Moab, Ammon, Edom and Sidon are named alongside those women, but the love is about people, not real estate.

That's the word. The LORD had told the Israelites, “You must not intermarry with them, for surely they will turn your hearts after their gods.” (1 Kings 11:2). It was a warning with the reason attached. When the LORD tells you something, He isn't hiding the ball.

Close to the neighborhood, but not the word. The LORD's warning wasn't about trading. He said, “You must not intermarry with them…” (1 Kings 11:2). It was about marriage, and He gave the reason right there: they would turn hearts after their gods.

Nobody's getting their passport taken away here, friend. The warning wasn't about travel at all. The LORD said, “You must not intermarry with them, for surely they will turn your hearts after their gods.” (1 Kings 11:2). So the word is intermarry.

True, and the LORD said it plainly. “You must not intermarry with them, for surely they will turn your hearts after their gods.” (1 Kings 11:2). That word “surely” is not a maybe. And the same verse says, “Yet Solomon clung to these women in love.”

This one is true, friend, so let me put the verse right in front of you. The LORD told the Israelites, “You must not intermarry with them, for surely they will turn your hearts after their gods.” (1 Kings 11:2). He gave the warning and the reason together. Then the text says that Solomon, Israel's king, clung to these women in love.

David it is. Verse 4 says Solomon, Israel's king, “…was not wholeheartedly devoted to the LORD his God, as his father David had been.” Same house and same family, but his heart went a different direction. That's why the text sets father and son side by side.

Nice try, friend, but Saul isn't in this verse. The text names Solomon's father, and he's David. Solomon, Israel's king, “…was not wholeheartedly devoted to the LORD his God, as his father David had been.” (1 Kings 11:4). The comparison is between a son and his own dad.

Absalom isn't named in this verse, friend. It says Solomon, Israel's king, “…was not wholeheartedly devoted to the LORD his God, as his father David had been.” (1 Kings 11:4). The man held up as the example is Solomon's father, David. So David fills the blank.

explanations.answer: He did evil in the sight of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes, and the text doesn't soften it. “So Solomon did evil in the sight of the LORD; unlike his father David, he did not follow the LORD completely.” (1 Kings 11:6). Solomon, Israel's king, had followed Ashtoreth and Milcom right before this. I think this is a heavy verse to read, friend.

explanations.answer: He made peace in the sight of the nations
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a nice press release, but it isn't what the text says. Verse 6 says, “So Solomon did evil in the sight of the LORD; unlike his father David, he did not follow the LORD completely.” The one watching is the LORD, not the nations. And the verdict is evil, not peace.

explanations.answer: He did justice in the sight of his people
explanations.explanation: The text goes the other way, friend. It says, “So Solomon did evil in the sight of the LORD; unlike his father David, he did not follow the LORD completely.” (1 Kings 11:6). Solomon, Israel's king, wasn't being measured by his people here. The LORD's sight is what counts, and the word is evil.

explanations.answer: A high place for gods of Moab and Ammon
explanations.explanation: That's the build. Solomon, Israel's king, “…built a high place for Chemosh the abomination of Moab and for Molech the abomination of the Ammonites.” (1 Kings 11:7). It went up on a hill east of Jerusalem.

explanations.answer: A storehouse for his gold and ivory
explanations.explanation: Nothing in these verses mentions a storehouse. Solomon, Israel's king, built something on that hill east of Jerusalem, and verse 7 says what: “…a high place for Chemosh the abomination of Moab and for Molech the abomination of the Ammonites.” So the build was for gods, not for gold.

explanations.answer: A stable for his horses and chariots
explanations.explanation: No stable is mentioned here, friend. Verse 7 says Solomon, Israel's king, “…built a high place for Chemosh the abomination of Moab and for Molech the abomination of the Ammonites.” That was on a hill east of Jerusalem. The build was for those two gods.

It reads like it might be true, but verse 8 goes further. Solomon, Israel's king, built the high place for Chemosh and Molech, and then “He did the same for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and sacrificed to their gods.” (1 Kings 11:8). So it wasn't only for Moab and Ammon. The text says all his foreign wives.

False is right, friend. After Solomon, Israel's king, built the high place for Chemosh and Molech, the text says, “He did the same for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and sacrificed to their gods.” (1 Kings 11:8). The phrase “…all his foreign wives…” is the giveaway.

explanations.answer: His heart had turned away from the LORD
explanations.explanation: The heart is the reason the text gives. “Now the LORD grew angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice.” (1 Kings 11:9). Solomon was Israel's king, and the LORD had appeared to him twice. I think that makes the turning even heavier.

explanations.answer: He had spent too much of Israel's gold
explanations.explanation: Money isn't the reason the text gives, friend. Verse 9 says the LORD grew angry with Solomon, Israel's king, “…because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel…” Gold isn't mentioned there at all. The heart is the problem, not the budget.

explanations.answer: He had grown too proud of his throne
explanations.explanation: The text never says anything about pride or a throne here. It says, “Now the LORD grew angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel…” (1 Kings 11:9). Solomon was Israel's king. The reason given is a turned heart.
Twice, yes. The LORD, the God of Israel, “…had appeared to him twice.” (1 Kings 11:9). That's Solomon, Israel's king. The text gives the exact count, friend, so there's no guessing needed.
Once would've been plenty, but the verse says more. The LORD, the God of Israel, “…had appeared to him twice.” (1 Kings 11:9). That's Solomon, Israel's king. So twice fills the blank.
The text gives a number here, friend, so often isn't the word for the blank. It says the LORD, the God of Israel, “…had appeared to him twice.” (1 Kings 11:9). That's about Solomon, Israel's king.

Kingdom is the word. The LORD said, “Because you have done this and have not kept My covenant and My statutes, which I have commanded you, I will tear the kingdom away from you and give it to your servant.” (1 Kings 11:11). Solomon was Israel's king. That's a serious sentence, friend.

Wisdom is a tempting guess for Solomon, Israel's king, but it's not what the LORD names. He says, “…I will tear the kingdom away from you and give it to your servant.” (1 Kings 11:11). The thing being torn away is the kingdom. The verse says nothing about wisdom here.

Riches are a fair guess for a king, friend, but the LORD doesn't mention them in this sentence. He tells Solomon, Israel's king, “…I will tear the kingdom away from you and give it to your servant.” (1 Kings 11:11). What's on the table is the kingdom itself, and a servant is the one who gets it.

That's who. The LORD said He would tear the kingdom away from Solomon, Israel's king, and “…give it to your servant.” (1 Kings 11:11). Notice the verse doesn't name the servant. I'll keep my mouth shut where the text keeps its own.

No foreign king gets handed anything in this verse. The LORD told Solomon, Israel's king, “…I will tear the kingdom away from you and give it to your servant.” (1 Kings 11:11). The one who gets it is Solomon's servant. Pharaoh is only mentioned earlier because of his daughter.

Sidon comes up in this passage, but not here. Women of Sidon are named in verse 1, and Ashtoreth is the goddess of the Sidonians in verse 5. The LORD's words in verse 11 are, “…I will tear the kingdom away from you and give it to your servant.” So it goes to Solomon's servant, not a king of Sidon.

True, and here's the LORD's own word: “Nevertheless, for the sake of your father David, I will not do it during your lifetime; I will tear it out of the hand of your son.” (1 Kings 11:12). Solomon, Israel's king, hears a hard sentence, and a “nevertheless” comes with it. The reason named is David. I think that one word “nevertheless” is worth underlining, friend.

This one is true, friend, so check the verse. The LORD says, “Nevertheless, for the sake of your father David, I will not do it during your lifetime; I will tear it out of the hand of your son.” (1 Kings 11:12). Solomon, Israel's king, wouldn't see it happen in his own lifetime. The tearing would come through his son.

One it is. The LORD says, “I will give one tribe to your son for the sake of My servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, which I have chosen.” (1 Kings 11:13). Just before that He says He won't tear the whole kingdom away from him. So the son keeps one tribe, friend.

Two is close, but the LORD gives a smaller number, friend. He says, “I will give one tribe to your son for the sake of My servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, which I have chosen.” (1 Kings 11:13). That's one, not two.

Ten is a big number, but it isn't the one in this verse. The LORD says, “I will give one tribe to your son for the sake of My servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, which I have chosen.” (1 Kings 11:13). That's the son's share: one tribe. Ten never shows up in these verses.

explanations.answer: It is the city He has chosen
explanations.explanation: Chosen, in the LORD's own words. He gives one tribe “…for the sake of My servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, which I have chosen.” (1 Kings 11:13). Even in a hard speech to Solomon, Israel's king, Jerusalem gets that line. Friend, that's worth a second look.

explanations.answer: It will be given to the servant
explanations.explanation: The servant gets the kingdom in verse 11, but Jerusalem is described differently. In verse 13 the LORD gives one tribe to Solomon's son “…for the sake of My servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, which I have chosen.” So the LORD's word about Jerusalem is that He has chosen it. Nothing says it goes to the servant.

explanations.answer: It will be left in ruins
explanations.explanation: Ruins isn't what the LORD says about Jerusalem, friend. He speaks of one tribe going to Solomon's son “…for the sake of My servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, which I have chosen.” (1 Kings 11:13). Jerusalem is named as part of the reason for that, and the LORD calls it the city He has chosen.
